utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If there are no procedural matters to be raised, then I would like to ask the usher to escort the witness in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Novakovic. May I remind you that You're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Jordash, are you ready to continue your examination .

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I have approximately 30 minutes of questions for you before other parties will want to ask you some questions. Could we have P2448 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, item number 11 in the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this document is presently under seal. However, in light of the Chamber's ruling with respect to the protective measures for the witness, I did review the document further and believe it would be okay to change its status to public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any response to ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In principle, we don't object. It's -- the only query I would have is whether there is a separate issue of protective measures for documents as contrasted with the protective measures for the -- any state security personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The bottom line is the same. Mr. Weber, perhaps it would be wiser for the Chamber just to review it as well, not that there's any distrust as far as you have reviewed, but we have our own responsibility and we will have to look at whether there are any BIA sources, BIA operatives, or any locations. But we'll certainly pay attention to change the status, as you suggested. Mr. Bakrac, any observations in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed. For the time being, the document remains under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, this, as I think you told us yesterday, is an Official Note of an interview which you conducted. And if we go to page 4 of the English and 4 of the B/C/S, we can see your name against the signature. And I presume that's your signature; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I think it's agreed again between us and the Prosecution that you interviewed Milan Lukic and the interview was conducted properly without coercion. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you say "no, no," you're saying no, it was not conducted -- well, were all formalities carried out in relation to interviewing Milan Lukic? Was it conducted properly from your perspective?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. All the legal regulations were observed and all the preconditions were met to conduct that interview with him in the way I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we go to page 4, or stay on page 4, at the end of -- or halfway down the page you offer an opinion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. At the beginning of item 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was that normal procedure for an operative following an operative interview, or -- to offer an opinion as to the veracity or reliability of the account offered?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That part of the document always reflects the opinion of the operative officer, how the interviewee had based during the interview, and how the operative views the veracity, the truthfulness of the source. You can't at the moment conduct all the checks as to what is true or not, but you can state your opinion on how the interviewee behaved and how truthful he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I take you, please, to page 2 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S, one-third of the page down where it begins: "During the long interview the source stated the following ..." the account that then follows, was this a verbatim account or a summary of what Milan Lukic said?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a primary document, the one they're looking at. And it was drafted based on an audio recording because the whole interviewee was recorded. At the beginning of the interview I warned Milan Lukic that it would be recorded and he had nothing to object to. And I state under quotation marks what Milan Lukic said, based on the audio recording. The interview was very long, one whole day. We started in the morning and ended in the evening, and that's why we keep the audio recording. In case we needed some more information from him, we would be able to continue that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Previous translation continues] ... is it a verbatim account or not?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is verbatim what he said and what I took from the audio recording and wrote down in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do I understand that to mean it's verbatim but it's not the whole of what he said during the day?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. You put in the document only what you think has any operative importance from that interview. Because there was a lot of talking there. He's not a very forthcoming person. And during the interview, it takes time to get him to talk about subjects that we were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, halfway down that page Lukic claimed that he was trained by Pupe and Zoran, Red Berets, Knindzas in Ilok. Did he ever claim that he was trained by Serbian DB in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well he said exactly what's written here. I was not familiar with that subject, so I quoted him in that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If he had said that he was trained by the Serbian DB, would you have been interested in that?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I wouldn't show any interest, but I would certainly write it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could Mr. Novakovic please be given 1D01072.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We'll give you a paper copy because I know that's your preference, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it's in Your Honours' chart at 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just as a reminder, I believe the Stanisic Defence has prepared a copy of this document that's unredacted as the 65 ter number .1. I don't know if we should be using that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the ruling of the Chamber was that the unredacted copy should be used and should be admitted into the evidence; whereas, at the end of the case, the redacted copies would be filed. That's ... in order to -- not to be overwhelmed by various versions of exhibits. Now we have access to it the unredacted copy, to the extent the document is shown to the public, of course, we could use a redacted version, although not the version that is or will be admitted into evidence, and I think it would be preferable if the witness, when he has a hard copy, that he gets the original, unredacted version. Is that what he received? Mr. Weber, that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed. [Trial Chamber and Registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, Madam Registrar asks to be -- to be informed in detail about which is the unredacted copy, because that's the one which will receive a number and which will be admitted into evidence; whereas the unredacted copies have you to deal with that a filing at a later stage. So please provide Madam Registrar with the exact number of the unredacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm afraid that we've got the redacted version on the screen. I'm afraid that Mr. Novakovic has got the redacted version as a hard copy. So perhaps if we could have the unredacted version on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I am afraid, Mr. Novakovic, you you'll have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Not to be shown to the public?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And does Madam Registrar know which number? Yes, there we are?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You have looked at this document before, Mr. Novakovic, and you've made some general comments in the chart at number 12. And I just want to pick up on one issue, which is the issue of the reaction of the VRS to the -- or VRS leadership to the arrest of Milan Lukic? If we look at page 2 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S, we can see there an account about Karadzic coming to Visegrad together with General Gvero by helicopter. And in paragraph 2, you'll see the following: "At this meeting" -- this is the meeting between Karadzic and representatives of Gorazde, Visegrad, Rogatica and Rude municipalities. [As read] "At the meeting Dr. Karadzic said that a Drina Corps would be formed and that the candidates for its commander were three persons from Serbia, of whom one was a general. He said that because of the situation a platoon of Milenko" - and it says here "Kasaric" but if one looks at the original, I think it says "Karisika" - "special police unit which would arrive from Zvornik and would say in Visegrad." He said that the decision had been made to replace Dr. Dusko Kornjaca and he was to blame for the situation in Kanicija [phoen] and so forth. Dr. Karadzic appears to, from this account, have control of Karisik; is that something that you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember that time, the unit of the special police was under the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just want to be clear. As far as you were aware at that time, Karasic's unit was under the command of the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska. Did it have anything to do with Serbia, as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly didn't. Because, at that time, it was a separate state. It happened on the territory of a different state.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just going further down to the page to the bottom of page 2 in the English and the top of page 3 of the B/C/S. There's an account there of Milan Lukic's father rallying soldiers in front of the command in Visegrad and calling out to the commander of the Tactical Group 1, Vinko Pandurevic, by saying, "You assigned him this task, that is, Milan Lukic, and just as you assigned him, now you get him out. If there is treason on your part, I shall kill you personally. After this, the soldiers went their own ways, after Pandurevic calmed them down by telling them this was an accidental arrest and that Milan Lukic would be released. Unofficially, during Dr. Karadzic's visit, I heard that he personally called President Milosevic about Lukic?" Are you able to comment on these remarks in relation to the reaction of the VRS leadership to the arrest by the Serbian MUP of Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you see from the document, I'd just like to note that I talked about this with the employer who is covering the territory nearer to Visegrad, and the sources we used were his sources. As the source mentions, after the -- after Dr. Karadzic left this meeting outside the building of the electrical company, many parents were gathered there, including the parents of Milan Lukic and they protested on that occasion against his arrest, and they were preparing a group or something to go and free him, after which he said that Milan Lukic was arrested in a state where law rules and if he is found to be innocent he will be released and given honours, but he also said that their approach was wrong, even though they were parents. It was inappropriate for them to react in that way. So what was stated here was stated by the source, and in the words of the source, he was present at the incident itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You said at the beginning of the answer to that question: "I'd just like to note that I talked about this with the employer who is covering the territory nearer to Visegrad." What did you mean by you talked to the employer? Who is the employer?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was saying I talked to my colleague about this. And I talked to Milan Lukic in the presence of that colleague, because that colleague had briefed me about Milan Lukic in the first place and the topics we would discussing with him. He covered that territory. I did not deal with that at the time. And these issues concerning Milan Lukic was under the 3rd Administration. It was the territory of a different state, so other employ employees, other colleagues covered that area and those kinds of activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you to have a look at 1D05068.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think we have a similar problem with redaction. We have an unredacted copy for the witness to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, I just wanted to reiterate our standing objection to the documents that are not presently on the Stanisic exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You've seen this document before, Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's at, Your Honours, page 4 and item 14 of the chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me take you, Mr. Novakovic, to the first page. And we can see a discussion there about the kidnapping of 17 citizens in Sjeverin municipality of Priboj, in the area of municipality Rudo, in the village Mioce. The security situation in municipality it's noted in Priboj is rapidly or has rapidly got worse. The 2nd of November, 1992. Is that something you can comment on?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the document, one can see that. I saw that. The document was shown to me by the Defence team. It was written --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm asking about whether you have any independent knowledge, independent from the document?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he talks about certain aspects of the security situation in the area of Priboj that resulted from the kidnapping of the people from Sjeverin. So he says it is disrupted and the interethnic situation in that area became more complex. And from this, we can see that even before the arrest of Milan Lukic, by the state leadership of Yugoslavia, sent a minister for human rights to that area --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to try to calm down that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now you see then in the fourth paragraph reference to a strong PJM unit from the MUP being sent to Sjeverin to strengthen a VJ unit. Do you know about --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Weber is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Prosecution objects as to foundation. This witness has been asked whether or not he has any independent knowledge about the document from what is in front of him. The witness then did not squarely answer that question. Instead reiterated a description of what's in the document. We don't need the document itself to be used with the witness if we're asking him about knowledge he has independent of it. This is leading and there is no foundation at this time for the witness's knowledge of what's being asked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yesterday the witness testified to the sending of a PJM unit to the region, in order to safe-guard Muslims, and that's what I'm asking the witness about, whether there is correspondence between what he said yesterday and what account is given in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is certainly a leading element in that. If a witness talks about A and you give him a document, say is there a link. There is, of course, a clear suggestion that there might be a link. So, If do you it in the most non-leading way possible, I would not stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just put aside the document and listen to my question for a moment, Mr. Novakovic. Put aside the document, Mr. Novakovic? The PJM unit you mentioned yesterday being sent to the territory covered by Uzice, what was it sent to do, who was it sent by, and where was it operative?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: T was sent by the Ministry of Interior, exactly to the area of Sjeverin to protect the Muslim population who were intimidated by this kidnapping. They started withdrawing from that area towards Priboj and it was sent to guarantee security, to provide reinforcements in that area. Sjeverin, there was a border unit of the army, and I know that in that period there occurred not exactly a clash but a difference of opinion because the army was against arresting Milan Lukic, and it was the military units who were in charge of securing the border; whereas, MUP units were there to protect law and order. And from this text, we see that members of the MUP also took into custody a military patrol. It was actually the special police unit that took into custody a military police unit who were looting the houses of Muslims who had fled to Priboj. So these units came there precisely to provide better security to Muslim citizens. Not long after that, in Prijepolje, which is not far from Priboj, special police units staff was established precisely because interethnic relations had been so disrupted by this kidnapping in this Uzice part of Sandzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. When you speak of a military police unit, which military formation did that police unit derive from?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphones could be lifted a little bit, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... talking about the military patrol from that border army unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could your microphone be a bit higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, we didn't receive your last answer? To whom did the military police unit belong?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the military unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In your last answer you mentioned [Overlapping speakers] ...?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military patrol? You mean -- oh. What I said was that the MUP units took into custody a military patrol. That is, a patrol that patrols the border area of Sjeverin, and it belongs to the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Just turning to page 2 of this document and the first -- sorry, page 2 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S. If you look at the paragraph: [As read] "The behaviour of Yugoslavia army's border units was highly incorrect and unprofessional one. The day Lukic was arrested some individuals from VJ unit which was protected Sjeverin openly threatened to use arms against MUP. Among soldiers there were a lot of those who used to be in paramilitary formations or they had some relatives within those units. "Today the members of MUP were taken into custody ... military patrol from Sjeverin ...," and so on. How did you learn about this incident? What's the source of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source of my knowledge in this particular case is this particular piece of information. But I know that people who worked in the territory, they came to the centre. They talked about those incidents, and it is from them that I learned of what was going on in the area of Sjeverin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me take you to another subject just briefly. Pauk. Sorry, before we get to Pauk, let me have a look at 1D05062. And it's in the chart at 6. Now, this payment list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just have caution just in case there's names of other individuals in here. If there is any way that we could please ask that it not be broadcast to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, that was remiss of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document not to be shown to the public. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, I'm just going to ask you about this document in a moment. First of all, in 1994, were you asked to go to work outside of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who requested that you go to work outside of Serbia; and where were you asked to go?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leadership of the service and my chief of service that I worked for requested that I go and assist the service of the Republic of Serbian Krajina due to the fact that in the western past of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, there were some cases of unrest. I volunteered to go together with two colleagues of mine, the same ones that you can see in the document. We were told that we would be involved in some counter-intelligence work in the area, in order to step up the level of security in that part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did this have anything to do with Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before my departure and my stint of over a month there, that operation was never mentioned under that name. The only thing that was said was that we would be dispatched there to assist the colleagues in Republic of Serbian Krajina in Kordun and Banija and that we would be dealing with counter-intelligence support for that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me then take you -- did you go there?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... did you first arrive; and what did you do upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I went from Uzice to Belgrade. I reported to the 2nd Administration there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: From the 2nd -- go on, sorry?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And together with the other two colleagues, we spent a whole day in an office. We were there till that evening before the departure. At that time there seemed to have been a lack of organisation or, at least, that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, I want to move forward just to deal with this briefly. I want to -- I'm interested in what happened when you arrived in the region. Where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in the region, I first arrived in Petrova Gora. I spent two days there, and from there, I went to Vojnic, and from Vojnic, I went to Slunj. I went to the shooting round of the technical military centre. That's where I was billeted, together with the two colleagues of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who did you report to, if anyone, in Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Petrova Gora, I arrived there by bus, from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who did you report to when you arrived in Petrova Gora? Did you report to anyone in Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived Petrova Gora, and I was billeted in a facility where we spent two days without talking to anybody. We did not have any communication with anybody until the meeting that took place on the 8th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Where was the meeting on the 8th of September?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meeting was held in Petrova Gora on the 8th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you sure it was the 8th of September?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the 8th of September. It was either the 8th or the 9th November.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who was at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the state security sector, Mr. Jovica Stanisic, and Franko Simatovic attended the meeting, together with the representatives of the service of the Serbian Army of Krajina, the service of the state security of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, the MUP of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and there were also the three of us who represented the State Security Service of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Based on the people that are being referred to now, this is something that could be of particular importance. We just would ask where did Mr. Jordash, the Stanisic Defence give us notice of a meeting containing this? Because we do not find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The summary notes that the witness was sent to Pauk by Jovica Stanisic from 1994 to 1995. He will describe his tasks and explain that he reported to Jovica Stanisic but usually to the DB Krajina. It's right we haven't actually said there was a particular meeting, but we would say it is implicit in that summary, that there is contact between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's call this the optimistic view, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, specifically meetings, specific meetings with these participants, of course, might be something that should not be implicitly referred to but perhaps explicitly. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, we didn't regard the meeting as particularly significant [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Inasmuch as it could have been a telephone call, it could have been a radio message. It simply [Overlapping speakers] ... the witness is going to describe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you have got an answer to your question. What next?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position would be that that notice is insufficient because of who was involved. Also, we would like to remind the Chamber: We did not receive a proofing note, we did not receive a statement. If Mr. Jordash, clearly by his question, specifically knew and has met with this witness prior to the testimony to bring up a specific meeting. We are prejudiced by lack of information like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you like to have that put on the record and then you will see how you will proceed. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You mentioned the service of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just if I could have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was the -- what happened at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first time anybody explained the reason for me and my colleagues being there. The meeting was chaired by Mr. Jovica Stanisic, and he told us that the meeting had been organised together security and intelligence segments of the services of the Serbian Army of Krajina, the MUP, and the state security. And the aim of the meeting was to unify all the intelligence about the goings on in the territory [Realtime transcript read in error "Territorial Defence"] and stepping up the security level in Krajina. The security was threatened by the refugees from the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia who arrived in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. As a result of that, the security situation was bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have a problem with the interpretation, page 18, line 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if have you a problem with the interpretation could you wait until the interpretation stops before raising this matter. You have a problem with page 18, line 23. Could you tell us what your problem is?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An institution was referred to, or, rather what was recorded was not mentioned by the witness himself. The name of the institution as recorded in the transcript was not mentioned by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you didn't hear that he was -- and I take it that it's, then, Territorial Defence which in your view was --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not mentioned. Now it is on the transcript. I think we should review that, whether the transcript and the translation is correct in this respect, and whether your ears, Mr. Petrovic, are better than the ears of others in this courtroom. Could we ask the witness to repeat the answer. You said the aim of the meeting was to unify all the intelligence. And could you then tell us what you after that said. To unify all the intelligence about ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To unify the entire intelligence about the security situation in the territory with refugees from the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have on the screen D447. I just want to look very briefly at the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, we -- you confirmed that these are the -- these were the locations of the refugee camps. First of all, are you able to give an assessment as to how many people were in these refugee camps at the time you were in the region?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure that accurately states the testimony - I'm checking right now - as to whether or not he said all of them were refugee camps, those locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What -- which of these, if any, were refugee camps, Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Refugee camps were in Batnoga, Turanj. Of those that are on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How many people were in Batnoga and Turanj?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Batnoga.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How many people in Batnoga?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, the international media referred to some 20- to 30.000 people in those camps. However, from what I saw, I would say that there were between 15 and 20.000 people there who had fled from Western Bosnia. It was impossible to establish the exact number because the situation changed daily. Every day new people came to the camp and overnight some people left the camp and returned to their original Western Bosnian territory. And that was the main problem at the time. Likewise, the media also referred to as many as 25.000 refugees in the refugee camp in Turanj. I myself never saw as many in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to give an assessment of how many in that area?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Batnoga, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, Turanj.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I didn't spend any considerable time there. What I was saying was that the estimates were the same for both of these camps. I actually never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Are you able to indicate the conditions of the refugees and the conditions of the camps?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, when I arrived in that area from my colleagues from the Republic of Serbian Krajina and as I told you, we were billeted in Slunj, I was astounded. Batnoga is not a village. It's not a location. Actually those were 12 hangars that had been used by the Agrokomerc company from Kladusa and the population lived there in very hard condition. My first impression that still lingers with me was when I saw hundreds of women sitting around those hangars cleaning their hair -- each other's heads from lice. This was a terrible sight. In other words, they were billeted in the hangars that had been previously been used by the Kladusa-based Agrokomerc, and I believe that that company had used those hangars to raise chicken there. But the most important thing for them was that they had roof over their heads because they had to flee from Kladusa and Western Bosnia because of war activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, there is some confusion. What you said in your last answer, is that all about Blatnoga, or that's at least what I read, Batnoga, I don't know which of the two it is, you're describing the situation there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The refugee camp, Batnoga, that's where refugees were billeted after having fled Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you earlier said that you actually never went there, you were referring to Turanj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never entered Turanj. With my group, I stayed in Slunj, and I was in charge of going ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you went to Batnoga, and you never went to Turanj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, these refugees, these Muslim refugees from the Autonomous Province of Bosnia, you were told at the meeting with Stanisic that they presented a security risk and your job was to help coordinate the intelligence in relation to that. What was the security risk as you were told or as you perceived it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could I please just have the transcript reference where he said exactly that, that the -- did he discuss the intelligence, but relating to the refugees being the risk. I see a general reference to something that could be considered that, but I object to the form of the question as leading based on the vague reference on page 18 at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's not a vague reference. It says: [As read] "... And the aim of the meeting was to unify all the intelligence about the goings on in the territorial Defence and stepping up the security level in Krajina. The security was threatened by the refugees from the Autonomous ..." I almost quoted verbatim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If refugees were a threat to the security, they could be considered to be a security risk. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, could you clarify what security risk or threat to the security was presented by the refugees as you were told, or as you perceived it?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was assigned to work with the team from Slunj, I was told that the refugee camp in Batnoga was active every day. Which meant that on a daily basis from the territory of Western Bosnia, which was under the occupation of the 5th Corps, new refugees arrived, and then it also happened that two, three, or five returned to Western Bosnia. You can only imagine what risk that was. Firstly, they fled to the Republic of Serbian Krajina and then they could move freely from the Batnoga camp, especially towards the Turanj camp. I don't know why they would do that, but I suppose they wanted to cross over to Croatia. But I can say that a lot of people from Batnoga would actually move to the Turanj camp. Let's say that the relative number was 40.000 but there were even more refugees in the two centres, and they were a security threat for that part of Krajina in Kordun because among those people who had fled there were also members of the 5th Corps, former members of the National People's Army of Western Bosnia, and in any case that was a security threat for the then-Republic of Serbian Krajina and its position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, I want to move swiftly through this then. How long did you stay in the region conducting these tasks?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came around the 4th of November and returned 15th, 15th December to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ever see Stanisic again in the region during your stay?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I saw him that one time at the initial meeting, that first meeting where it was -- which discussed why we were there, why we had come, and it was a joint meeting of all security services, security branches represented at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: With the information you gathered, who did you report it to?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the information we would collect on the ground, my two colleagues and I, jointly with two representatives from the security service of the Republic of Serbian Krajina were reported to the service of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. Our main task was to provide this information to them because they collated it. And I would occasionally inform Belgrade as well, namely, the 2nd Administration through the secure communications we had at Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's return to the payment list very quickly. 1D05062, not to be shown to the public. You've told us -- as this document comes up you told us that the two gentlemen on the list were the two that went with you to Petrova Gora. Were you paid per diems during that time; and does this reflect that?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Any journey outside the centre entitled people to per diem. This is how we received per diem, the two of us, and this is a receipt.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In the chart at number 6 -- there's no need for you to turn it up. But in the chart at number 6, you say that the payment had nothing to do with you working for the PJM despite the fact it says that on the document. Do you know why this document would note PJM, even though you were not, as you've told us, working for the PJM?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to explain, although I'm not a financial expert. At the time when interethnic relations were disrupted in Sandzak, in Kosovo, and elsewhere, the Presidency of the Republic of Serbia made a decision that special police units, the PJM, would be paid in this way, in per diem. In fact, they received salaries in their original units when they were employed but when they would go into the field, on field missions, to areas where security was disrupted, they would be paid in the form of per diem, in keeping with that decision of the Republic of Serbia, or, rather, its Presidency. Since the State Security Service at that time was a sector of the Ministry of Interior, the only way we could pay our operative officers when they went outside in other areas of the Republic of Serbia or even outside of Serbia, we were paid through this modality, which was a legal modality for paying their costs and work on field missions. From this, can you see that every centre, including the centre where I worked, had a financial officer and a treasurer, who dealt with the financial aspects of the operation in everything concerning the employees of that centre. He was responsible to the centre but also on a parallel track to the financial service of the administration. They would get a budget for a month, and an operative worker could go and field missions within the centre for his regular -- for -- for per diem from that budget. But if he went outside the centre he would be paid per diem from the budget from the administration in Belgrade, and that's -- that's what you can see from this paper, that this was signed by an officer in Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which administration --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness, I believe, answered the question that my learned friend Mr. Jordash has just started asking, so I will refrain from comment. I see that my learned friend is just about to ask this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then we would receive the answer twice. That's the major risk we're in. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which administration was the -- was on the parallel track with the administration from the centre. Let me simplify that. You spoke about the issue arising from the financial officer within the centre and then a parallel track with an administration in Belgrade. Which administration in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The administration in charge of financial issues in Belgrade was the 8th Administration of the DB at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Milan Prodanic. What was his position at the time of this payment, this --

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the chief of the 8th Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And just to wrap up this subject, what did this -- did this have anything to do with Jovica Stanisic, the paying of per diems to you when you were in the field, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did the payment of per diems to you when you were in the field have anything to do with Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the chief of the service. He had nothing to do with this. This is standard procedure whenever employees go outside their local area. It had to do something with the chief of the financial administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I try to understand this answer. From what I understand you were instructed to go there and it was explained to you in a meeting with Jovica Stanisic what your task was. And as a consequence, you are paid per diems by the budget, not your own budget. So to say he has got nothing to do with it, of course, he was not involved in the -- that's what I understand from your answer. He was not involved in paying out -- or administrative matters in relation to the per diems. But what he had to do with it, that, as a consequence of your assignment by him to go there, you received these per diems from this central budget and not your own budget. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just add to what I said earlier to try to be clearer. I've said I'm not an expert in financial matters but I'm able to understand that much. At that time, by virtue of a decision made by the Republic of Serbia, a certain fund was established for payments to the members of the special police unit who went on field missions in the territory of -- of the Republic of Serbia, and every member of the State Security Service, that is, the special police unit, was paid from that fund, whenever they went to other areas to assist. In the same way, state security employees also went to other areas, mainly border areas where local personnel had less experience and people from the centre were sent there to assist them. But the state security, being part of the MUP of Serbia, the only legal way of paying these workers, was from this fund, and I suppose the service requested funding for its own personnel from this fund. People who were in charge of finances and logistics within the service were in the 8th Administration, which had its chief. He was in charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not seeking the details about how it was organised but when you said it had nothing to with Stanisic, it was a consequence of being assigned the task to go there that had as a consequence that you were paid per diems out of this fund. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are absolutely right. As a staff member, I was assigned to those tasks, and that triggers certain procedures in finance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I note the time, Your Honour. I'm sorry it has taken so long. I would like another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take a break, I have one follow-up question. Mr. Novakovic, you were asked whether being sent there was part of Operation Pauk. Your answer was, "During the month or during the six weeks I was there, that the operation was never mentioned by that name." Now, my question to you is: Is -- apart from what was said during this six weeks, can you tell us positively that it was not part of Operation Pauk, or do you have any other knowledge which would either link your presence to or not link your presence to Operation Pauk, if, at least, you know what Operation Pauk stands for? Perhaps we start with the last question: Are you familiar with Operation Pauk and what it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learned later on that the Operation Pauk was a military operation to get the population that had fled to return to the area of Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now then we go to the other question. When you learned about Operation Pauk, did you ever learn anything about a link between your presence, your assignment to go there, and Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that while I was still there. I realized that our activities, the activities of the intelligence group Slunj were part of or serving the operation aimed at getting the population from Western Bosnia to return. Because in talking to the citizens in that area that crossed from one side to another all the time, we found out what was going on, which forces were deployed there on both sides, et cetera, what the movements were, and we informed the State Security Service of Serbia regularly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I then well understand your answer that your presence there was related to the operation, which you later learned to be Operation Pauk, but the name of which was never mentioned when you were in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was there in early December, I never once heard the moniker Pauk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that doesn't answer my question. It is only part of the question. You never heard the operation being called Operation Pauk; but what you later learned about Operation Pauk, this military operation, that was the operation in relation to which you performed your tasks. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the sense of collecting intelligence. That was my assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Jordash, before we take the break, you made an observation earlier in relation to 1D01072, which is the Official Note of the 2nd of November. You said it was about a unit of -- in English Kasarik's [sic] unit, Milenko Kasarik's unit, and then you referred to your original and then you said in the original it says Kasarika. Would it be possible that Milenka Kasarika is the genitive case for Milenko Kasarik? So you suggested there was something not correct, not accurate, in the translation, because you said in the original it refers to Kasarika, and I am just asking myself whether there was any inaccuracy or whether you were reading in the original the genitive case, which, of course, is translated into English as "Kasarik's".

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you made a comment on the difference so, therefore, I would expect you to have thought about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I think there is no dispute that this man [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can ask the interpreters is "Milenka Kasarika" the genitive case of what is translated as "Kasarik's". And I'm listening to the English channel at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're normally not allowed to pronounce such judgements off the cuff. But it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I could ask you not about the original but whether Milenka Kasarika is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Genitive, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore there seems to be no inaccuracy in "Kasarik" or "Kasarika".

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, and I think there is no dispute that this is Milenko Karisik, who is part of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Kasarik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've only ever seen it written Karisik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may have made a mistake there. But at least we don't have to further pay attention to the -- to the suggestion of there being an inaccuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. And in the absence of the witness I can provide a little more context as to why I asked that question, if it will assist Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I was interested in your observation that the original says whether it is Kasarik or Karisika, but it was suggested there was an inaccuracy and appears to no [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the only thing I wanted to deal with. We take a break and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, before we continue, and, Mr. Novakovic, our apologies for the two or three or four minutes we might need with another matter. The Chamber would like to, first of all, briefly deal with the urgent Stanisic Defence motion for video-conference link. We have received a courtesy copy of the Prosecution's response. Has that been filed, meanwhile or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe it was filed last evening, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Last evening, okay. Then we -- has the Simatovic Defence any response to this motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honours. We leave it to the Trial Chamber's judgement and to the parties. As far as we are concerned, we have nothing against the videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber has considered, as we now know, all the submissions, because there is no Simatovic submission. The Chamber grants the request for the use of video-conference link to hear the evidence of Witness DST-052; reasons to follow. And, Mr. Jordash, the timing of this request was not perhaps the best, because you know exactly how much time it takes to prepare for a videolink conference, and, at the same time, the medical condition seems to be there already for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The problem has been that despite all best endeavours by our investigator to contact the witness, the witness was constantly responding with, I'm ill, I can't deal with this at the moment. Which is why it is late. But we do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because it may cause some additional problems. That is also the reason why we deal with it now, at this very moment, so that the Registry is informed without delay and that the preparations for the videolink can start from now on. Mr. Jordash, are you ready to continue with your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, Mr. Jordash will have some further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to move very quickly through the last few subjects if I can, Mr. Novakovic. Just to complete the issue of your stay in and around Batnoga, why did you leave the area?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay in Batnoga, I was interested in information relevant to the deterioration of the interethnic situation in that area. I conducted a large number of interviews together with my colleagues from the Republic of Serbian Krajina relating primarily to the security situation, to the problems that increased security risks in that area. I suppose that among that information there was also intelligence that was new to the leadership of the service in Belgrade, and I received instructions to leave the area urgently the very next day because my life is at risk. I got that instruction through the service in the Republic of Serbian Krajina; namely, that I and my two colleagues were to return to Belgrade the very next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was it communicated to you why or from whom your life was at risk?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't told that. The way I understood it was that the only reason could be my field-work. To be honest my colleagues and myself put in a lot of effort to -- into the daily reporting of the events in the area. You know, the area was a mixed area and what we saw in the field among the population of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, the two groups had years long ties. They had developed all sort of relationships and there were additional activities that compounded the risk, like smuggling and other things. Whenever I went to the supply point, either me or my colleague, I informed my superiors in Belgrade about that. I don't know whether that increased the risk of my stay. In any case, the order was that I should urgently return to Belgrade the following day, and I did that, both myself and my two colleagues did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of December, we returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In May and -- or May or June of 1995, were you called upon by Jovica Stanisic to do anything? To conduct any particular task?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the centre chief, I was informed that I should set out for the mission that had been given to me by the chief of the service. I was supposed to go to the area of Visegrad, where I was supposed to take part in dealing with the hostage crisis. That was the situation that prevailed around that time in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you speak to Stanisic directly; and what instructions were given to you either directly or indirectly?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received instructions indirectly from the centre chief. I was to go on the mission and get in touch with the representatives of the service of the Republika Srpska in Visegrad and they were supposed to provide me with more information. Until the hostages were handed over, I never saw or talked to Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who were the hostages?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in the territory of Visegrad, I got in touch with the representatives of the state security of the Republika Srpska. We were waiting for the hostages to arrive, and they were supposed to be brought by the Herzegovina Corps of the Republika Srpska. According to what I saw, there were about 30 or 40 members there. I don't know who they belonged to exactly, but most of them belonged to the Ukrainian contingent. Some of them were Spaniards, i.e., belonging to the Spanish contingent of UNPROFOR. And I'm not sure whether the rest were French. Talking from this time distance, it's hard to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you do anything in relation to the hostages? What was your task?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task was to take them over. I had a bus with a driver from the secretariat of the interior. My task was to get in touch with the representatives of the service of the Republika Srpska. They were supposed to hand -- mediated in the hand-over of the hostages from the Army of Republika Srpska. My duty was to put them on the bus and take them across the territory of the Republika Srpska, up to Zvornik, i.e., up to the point where they would leave the territory of the Republika Srpska and enter the territory of Serbia. The situation in Visegrad was not really normal. People in uniforms had been brought to Visegrad and we could see that they belonged to the various contingents of UNPROFOR, that they were of different ethnicities. And they told me, "They're yours, take them." And I said, "I can't do that. I have to make a list. How can I take over the people without their names?" And I remember that there the situation was very tricky and the name of the place was Butkova Stijena. I took over the group of hostages, and every member of the hostage group entered the bus and I read out their names. I put their names on -- on a separate list, and finally, the representative of the Herzegovina Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska signed the list confirming that those, indeed, were the men in question. I put them on the bus. Together with us was a representative of the state security of the Republika Srpska and a member of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness notification for this -- for Mr. Novakovic indicates that he testified to the role of transport of hostages from Zvornik not Visegrad to Novi Sad. There's a lot of details that are now coming into the record. We -- if it's being offered like this at this time now apparently he wasn't in Zvornik, he was in Visegrad, we ask for a substantial foundation as to the individuals that he is meeting with, when did this happen. Right now he is testifying generally about a bunch of different things, meetings, transport of people. So we're objecting to the foundation at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think they went from Visegrad to Zvornik and then left the -- so, at least Zvornik appears. But, Mr. Jordash, if could you shed some additional light on it, then it might assist Mr. Weber in understanding the evidence a bit better.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which route did you take with the hostages from Visegrad? Where did you take them to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Weber is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, first of all, let me see ... When was it? Who were they; that's the first question. Because we're talking about hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When did you attend Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been either the 1st or the 2nd of June, as far as I can remember, I -- I mean. I believe it was the 2nd of June. I really can't remember the exact date after such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Fair enough. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we are talking about the hostage crisis. Who were the hostages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, after such a long time, I took over hostages who were nationals of Ukraine. I believe that there were also Spaniards and French, and the whole group comprised about 30 or 40 men. It was a long time ago. It's very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think this identifies sufficiently; we have all heard about a hostage crisis before and taking over of hostages and we have heard about the role that Mr. Stanisic may have played and apparently the questions and the answers are about that same event.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. That is appreciated. However, this witness was testifying actually to particular arrival and meetings with particular officials of Republika Srpska once he got to Visegrad. If we could have some foundation as to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not really sure what my learned friend wants in terms of foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's -- if -- Mr. Weber, if you have any additional questions there you can raise the matter in cross-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you take the hostages from Visegrad; and, if you did, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took the hostages over from Visegrad and the route we took led through the territory of the Republika Srpska up to Zvornik. There is a border crossing there, I don't know whether it was Karakaj or Sepak; in any case, we crossed a bridge there, and in the territory of the Serbia the then-chief of service, Mr. Jovica Stanisic, and Franko Simatovic waited for us. I believe that Mr. Vlado Dragicevic was also there and there was some security detail. I can't give you the exact time but I remember that on the bridge where we took -- brought the hostages, Mr. Stanisic held a press conference because there was a huge number of journalists there. I don't remember the exact date. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just, finally, Mr. Witness, just returning to 1995 and the issue of protection of Muslims in Uzice region. Following the massacres in Srebrenica, was there any issue which arose as a result of Muslims fleeing those events?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of the Uzice centre in that period, there was a large influx of population from the area of Zepa to the area of the Uzice centre. I cannot recall the exact time-frame. I think it could be August.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did any military Muslim formation cross over into Uzice territory at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the entire 7 Assault Brigade crossed over in the area of Jagostica and the other part in the Drina valley. And they were escorted by the Army of Yugoslavia and taken deeper in Serbia, in the area of Jagosko Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did that have anything to do with the DB?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, the service monitored those movements. Of course, it knew that they were taken in and escorted by the army and the MUP to Vranesko Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Escorted by the army and the MUP. Were they -- last question, Mr. Novakovic. Were they treated well, this Muslim formation, this military formation of the 7th Assault Brigade when they fled the events and entered Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. They were treated in keeping with international law. I believe the ICRC was present from the start. They were touring that area. And, later on, representatives of the BH government came to visit. Those people were asked who wanted to go where, and very few of them wanted to return to Bosnia. Most of them wanted to go to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did the DB monitor that?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The DB was able to monitor from the moment when the refugee centre was established. But I believe there was a team from the public security sector there, and the DB people joined in, sort of, because of the presence of such a large number of people on the ground. But the admission process and the escorting was handled by the MUP mainly, because the border unit of the army escorted them only to Vranesko Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Petrovic, would it be you who will cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us a time estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I will need about 30 minutes. Looking at the clock, I think we're close to the break so I think perhaps it's better to go to the break first and then begin with my cross-examination. But, in any case, I'm ready, whenever you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at you, Mr. Jordash, and I'm also looking at Mr. Stanisic. If we take the break now, then we would have -- yes, then we would have approximately 75 minutes left. Perhaps that's the better idea. Mr. Weber, could you give us an indication for scheduling purposes on how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on a lot of things that accumulated during the examination, it will be a rough estimate at this stage. High side, four hours; low side, three hours, would be our estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take the break now. And you can start your cross-examination, Mr. Petrovic, after the break. We resume at 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, I would like to briefly address Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash, if you want to have a videolink, you have to give a date. I mean, we can't ask the Registry to prepare a videolink without knowing the scheduled date and you have to arrange with the other witnesses the way you deem appropriate. But we can't just say somewhere in the next two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not really following why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked for a videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That means someone has to be available at -- the premises have to be there. Everything has to be prepared. We need a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I -- I hadn't realized that we had got to the point where we had not given a date at a time when we ought to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed by the Registry that when the Stanisic Defence were asked for date that they didn't get an answer. Okay. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... if that is true, then I apologise and I'll remedy that immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, without delay. Mr. Petrovic, sorry to interrupt you, but videolinks are always urgent. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I fully appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Novakovic. I have a few questions for you with regard to your evidence given so far. First of all, I would like to follow up on the last subject that you discussed and that was the 7th Brigade and its exit from Zepa. Do you know if there were pressures on the part of the -- the Army of the Republika Srpska for those people who had crossed over to Serbia to return to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pressure of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The Army of the Republika Srpska or some other bodies of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no pressures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, we have a problem with the interpretation. Page 61, line 13. With your leave I can repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any pressures on the part of the Army of the Republika Srpska or some other bodies of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such pressures. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The answer is the same that you provided a minute ago but that was not recorded nicely in the transcript. And could you please look at D156. I would like to call up the document in e-court on the screen. Witness, this is a very short document, only one page long. Could you please look at it and then I will have a couple of questions concerning that document. Witness, sir, are you ready for my questions?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, under 1 in this document, some features and towns are mentioned in the valley of the Drina river. Can you just confirm for us that all the towns and facilities and features are on both banks of the Drina River which means both on the Bosnian and the Serbian sides of the river. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if it is correct that in 1992 and later on the JNA firstly and then the Army of Yugoslavia provided security in the course of the Drina river bordering on Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which troops were used to do that at the beginning while the JNA still existed and, later on, when the security border -- border security was maintained by the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that there was a border unit of the army, especially at the beginning, they provided security for the Perucac dam above Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, did it come a time when the territory of the Republic of Serbia was immediately and directly threatened by combat activities from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was directly threatened from the territory of Skelani. When the attack on the bridge between Skelani and Bajina Basta was launched, and when shelling started and when shells started reaching the town itself. I believe that a few people even got killed on the bridge itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the shells from the Muslim positions fell on the town of Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I can't remember the exact date, but I believe that that was at the moment when the offensive in Skelani was launched in the direction of the bridge in Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was that in January 1993 or, rather, in early 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I believe that it was in early 1993 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether on that occasion in Bajina Basta and in the relevant area there were visits by the president of the government and the Ministry of Interior because of the situation?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. After the shelling of Bajina Basta and the attack on the bridge in Skelani. The minister of the interior and the prime minister arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And the situation in the territory of Skelani and Bajina Basta was that something of special interest to you and your service?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That was a direct threat on the territory which was within the catchment area of our centre and I believe that the leadership of the service was informed about the situation on the ground. A document that we saw a while ago speaks about the activities on the bridge and the spillover of the front line onto our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you, at that moment, reinforce the presence of your operatives in the territory of Bajina Basta in the general area at the moment when these events were taking place?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes precisely. That happened. A few employees went to assist on the territory. They came from the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I have to ask you to make a pause between my question and your answer, we speak the same language and the interpreters are finding it very difficult to interpret everything. If I keep silent that doesn't mean that I'm waiting for you to expand on your answer, I'm just waiting for the interpretation to be over so that I can start putting my next question to you.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the employees who were sent to Bajina Basta. If you do, we will move into private session so can you tell us. Just tell us if you know.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
