utterances.text: In that period, I know from our territory an operative officer from Arilje went there, and one operative officer from the centre in Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the names?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know one name. I'm trying to recollect the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can we move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we spoke yesterday about the hydro power plant in Perucac. Can you tell us, if you know, in terms of ownership to whom does this hydro power plant belong? Is it a joint ownership between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it is Serbia's, but the building itself is on the border between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. But do you know about the transformer of that plant. On which side of the Drina river is it?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the distribution plant. It's on the territory of Serbia. It is in a place called Beserovina and it is serving most of Serbia's territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you have any evaluation of the security risk to this installation and the dam itself. How did you assess the security situation around the hydro power plant?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The DB centre in Uzice, and there is a document about it, had information that the bridge nearby and the plant in Beserovina would be bombed. We even knew from where exactly on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina it was going to be targeted. And then the army got the assignment to defend the dam as well as the distribution plant within the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you know, can you tell us where were those artillery weapons located. You were mentioning a location somewhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina from which this dam was threatened. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is in the area of Skelani, and I believe the document specifies the exact location. We can look at the document if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the document where you provided your comments?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you could assist us, tell us which document you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 7 in this binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we have shown 1D5065, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, is that the document?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the document. I believe it's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn the page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, in the second paragraph, you can see the exact... oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you mean the gun that disappeared from Potocari, moved to Skelani?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, hidden on the property of the Memici brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And from that location, one could directly target both Bajina Basta and the hydro power plant.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly the distribution facility. That was their target in Beserovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago, Witness, that the army intervened eventually in the situation in the Skelani in 1992. Do you know who and how?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you turn to page 3, you will see that the army was involved in defending the hydro power plant in Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's leave the document aside. Just try to answer my question to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the army was engaged to protect the dam specifically that was on the border itself, and it was threatened by the constant exchange of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at P599.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this document not be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you look at the witness -- at the document on the screen, Witness. If you are done with the first page, we can look at the second one.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can we show the witness the second page. Please only look at the signature. We don't need to read the whole document, not to waste time.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go to page 1 again so I can ask you about two allegations from that page. The document was signed by the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, Zivota Panic, but I'm interested in only paragraph 2 that reflects the situation on the ground, the opening of fire, the throwing of explosive devices on privately owned buildings, et cetera. Just confirm, please, what is stated in this document, is it consistent or not with your knowledge about the situation on the ground at the time when the document was written in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's consistent completely with the information available to the service about the situation in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: One more thing: You mentioned today the setting up of MUP staffs. We see that an order is given here to set up MUP staffs and the organs responsible for their establishment are the ministries of republics. The staff in Prijepolje, is it consistent with this?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- you know there was a staff in Prijepolje. Do you know if there was a staff in Bajina Basta, for instance, or in other areas at risk?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure now whether I remember or not. There was one in Bajina Basta, but I remember about Prijepolje because of Sjeverin, Strpci and that situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Those staffs were set up to monitor the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And to boost security.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And those staffs were formed as part of the public security sector of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I would now like to move to a new subject. You said yesterday that some political parties in the Republic of Serbia began to develop militant wings using volunteers who had just returned from wars or had done stints in various wars. Which militant wings?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There are too many microphones on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer now?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, go on if the Trial Chamber allows.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Priboj, we noticed specifically that the Serbian Popular Defence is present with their paramilitary unit, White Eagles that came and went from wars. Then the party SPO had two wings of Serbian Guards, also a paramilitary unit. Then the Serbian Chetnik Movement was a paramilitary unit that flirted both with the SPO and the Serbian Radical Party. That's what I remember about the Serbian side in our area of these units of passing through our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you explain why the activities of these paramilitary units were of interest to you and where exactly lay the danger to the security of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that militant wings and the arming of such units posed a threat to Serbia in itself. They went to wars and they came back with weapons. In the programmes and platforms of these political parties it was stated that what they could not achieve by parliamentary means they would do otherwise and that would create danger for peace within Serbia and that's why we needed to monitor the activities of those militant and the potential sources of new paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In order to gather intelligence on these paramilitary units, you had to have sources able to provide such information; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was it necessary for those sources to be inside, to be able to provide good information about the activities of these groups?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the only way to get such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us the connection between such an inside source and the operative who runs that source, the controller?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's perhaps important to emphasise that members of those paramilitary units in our area were people from criminal gangs, people bent on crime, people without fixed employment, which made it possible for them to go frequently to wars. Our operative could approach such a person in their own environment, so we monitored the activities of those people in our own area among the people who did not hide their affiliations to paramilitary formations. At that time national passion was running high, especially among those people who were members of paramilitary units although their activities ran mainly in another direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the relationship of your service with such people. So you needed people who were either part of those units or very close to those units?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. Because only in that way could we get good information from the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I would like to ask you now about your stay in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, a few points. You told us earlier today what you were interested in. Could we just clarify your relationship with the State Security Service of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Was your relationship with them one of subordination, of co-operation, of something else?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a relationship of collaboration, joint work on improving the security situation in the area of the RSK. It was not one of subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What does this co-operation imply, in terms of information procured by members of one or another service?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We worked jointly. Throughout my stay in the RSK, we worked together with members of the RSK service. We shared information about the assignments we had accomplished, and we reported primarily to the centre of -- of the RSK service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, were you interested in the smuggling channels that existed in the territory of the northern part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, when we talked to the refugees in the refugee camp, we always asked them there was any smuggling going on in that area, the smuggling of all sorts of goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn something about the possible smuggling?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we reported on that, regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned earlier today the significance of those people who would come to the camp and leave on a daily basis. How did that reflect on the overall security situation in that part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you -- or let me put it this way. For example, five people leave the camp one day and -- and two days later, two of them return, which means that they were very well informed about the security situation in the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the same danger exist in -- with regard to the units of the Army of Republika Srpska? Was their loyalty jeopardized? Was there a possibility that any of the troops could shift over to the ranks of the 5th Corps? Was there an imminent danger of that?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was such a danger. AP Western Bosnia was the official army, and the troops would defect from there and join the 5th Corps. That was a security threat because they had a state in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina together with other refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in intelligence sense were you also interested in Fikret Abdic and his entourage? Did you gather intelligence about that?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the state security of Serbia and I spent sometime in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I could see for myself that Fikret Abdic and his colleagues had contacts with the representatives of Croatia and the Federation, that they participated in trade negotiations and other types of negotiations. I monitored those activities as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you also gather intelligence about the activities of the Croatian forces in view of the location of the refugee camps and that part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in general terms?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I was, the contacts with the Croatian side were fewer and further between, unlike in Turanj. But in any case, we did collect intelligence with regard to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What kind of intelligence did you collect? What did you find interesting as an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally, people from Batnoga moved to Turanj and some of them even moved to Croatia and we found that interesting as a potential source of information on something that could pose a security threat for the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session. Mr. Petrovic, I would like to inform you that the -- all three Judges have lost more or less -- are lost more or less in terms of what the relevance of all these details are.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try and focus on something that I believe will be relevant and I can also explain the relevance of my questions so far, if you think that that should be necessary. If not, I can leave it for a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can do it in one line, it would be appreciated. Otherwise, save it for a -- another day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness was an intelligence officer. I would like to find out what kind of intelligence he gathered and what was the subject of interest of the service that dispatched him to the Republic of Serbian Krajina. What was the essence of his work. That was the information that I tried to elicit from him because it is of some interest for my client. However, I shall drop that and move onto another topic. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know whether a communications centre was located in Petrova Gora? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a communications centre at Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Ranko Tadic is?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name does ring a bell, but I never met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what he did, what he was responsible for?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he had something to do with the communications centre and maintaining communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please look at 65 ter 4983.1, page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at the list of names and tell us whether you recognise any of the names besides the name of Ranko Tadic; and also if you know any of them, could you tell us what they did.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I recognise the name of Nikola Varda. And I believe that he was an electronic surveillance and reconnaissance and communications, and he worked at the communications centre himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while we're still in private session, could you please tell us whether you know anything about

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you told us about the intelligence work and you said that you were a member of the administration -- of the intelligence administration as of November 1995, if I'm not mistaken. How did you gather intelligence? You testified about interviews with sources, associates and so on and so forth. What was the significance of intelligence gathering by way of other means, primarily technical means. Can you explain briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Petrovic switch his microphone off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our service, we valued a live source the most. However, during the war, we also obtained a lot of intelligence by technical means, and that was also a valuable source of intelligence for us, although we were not well equipped, due to the great effort of the 2nd Administration, we engaged in some offensives, and we managed to have a lot of breakthroughs in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. That was a large contribution when it comes to the reporting to the leadership of our service and the leadership of the state. I'm talking about the electronic surveillance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Weber, are you ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did you first meet with members of the Defence to discuss your testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I met them in the month of March this year. I met them in Belgrade, some members of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On how many occasions have you met with the Defence to discuss your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three times, I believe. The last time I met them immediately before my arrival here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when these occasions were after March 2011?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly switch off your microphone, Mr. Weber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that in March, I had those meetings, but I don't know when. I don't know on which dates. The last time was very recently, immediately before my arrival here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who was present during these meetings?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were present were Tatjana Cmeric, Tatjana Zafirovic, and Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't hear the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last name?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Wayne Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you see, or were Jovica Stanisic or Franko Simatovic present during any of these occasions?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During these meetings with the Defence, did you discuss the testimony which you have presented this week?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you shown documents that you have commented on during your testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was shown most of the documents. And as for the rest of the documents in the binder, I saw them when I arrived here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: To understand your answer clearly, were you shown documents that are in that comment chart prior to your arrival in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them I did. The rest I saw here. And I believe that in my comments accompanying the documents can also tell you exactly which of the documents I only saw here, when I arrived in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So when you said "the first time that I saw a document," that corresponds to you seeing for the first time here in The Hague; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Based on the rather specific questions that have been asked to you today, is it correct that the Defence took notes of what you told them during these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were these notes kept in typewritten form? In other words, was the Defence typing as you spoke?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so that, yes, notes were kept. I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I see that you have with you here today and you have brought into the courtroom a folder. And I can see from here that, as part this folder, the contents contain handwritten notes. Are those your personal handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just a piece of paper, some notes that I took yesterday and continued taking them today just to be able to focus on your question. I have a decision of the government with the topics that I can discuss, and I have this binder with the documents, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Would you be willing to provide that spiral notebook with the handwritten notes and that decision from the government to the Court Usher in order for it to be distributed to the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Registry could actually take possession of the spiral binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Before that happens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- I think it would be appropriate for my learned friend to explain why that should take place and what the relevance is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Throughout the testimony here today I have watched the witness repeatedly look at these notes while he's answering questions. There is clearly information on them and he has been consulting them throughout his course of his testimony. We would like to know what's in front of the witness while he's testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness explained, I think, that he made these notes. Could I -- I can't read it. How many notes is that? That one page, half a page, ten pages? Just on the first page of that. And did you make those notes in court here or in between during the breaks? When did you make these notes, just one page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When somebody asks me questions, I just made a note of the topics. You're free to take a look. It is no secret. And this is the decision of the government relieving me of keeping the state secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... can I indicate I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the waiver from the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, the -- looking at the kind of notes and the explanation of the witness, the Chamber considers that the witness is not under any obligation to give those notes to you at this moment. That's one. Second, if the decision of the government would not be otherwise available to you, then, of course, the witness is willing to give it, then -- but I do not know. I take it that that's the kind of decisions that we've seen before. There are no protective measures. The witness has not, on any subject matter, invoked any duty not to answer the -- the questions. That is -- so if you really need that decision, then, Mr. Jordash --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just -- two things very briefly. One, just for the record, we don't accept that the witness was consulting these notes on a constant basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whatever it is, the ruling of the chamber is clear. The witness is not under any obligation to give these notes, in view of his explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And secondly, that we don't, if the witness wants to, we don't object to those notes being shown to Your Honours or the parties. It is just so that the record is clear on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, of course, if you write down what the subject matter of the question is, then consulting the note would mean that you tried to remind yourself of what was asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that to extent, it would not be very useful to make these notes and not consulting them but only for this very limited purpose. Mr. Weber, do you insist on the decision of the government to be handed out to you at this moment by the witness, or at least would you -- do you have no other way of --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the printed decision there's no problem with that. But the witness has been writing today during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's a ruling on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We would like the notes. The decision is -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is not under any obligation to give the notes. If you want to give them, Mr. Novakovic, you're free to do so. But the Chamber is not insisting on you giving the notes you made to Mr. Weber. If you say, let him have a look at it, then please feel free to provide them to Mr. Weber. What's your decision? To give them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing that I have here is, for example, when I entered the court, when I left the court, when the breaks were. These are my notes, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. If you say I'll give them to Mr. Weber, they will be presented to him. They will be copied. And if you say, I'm not inclined to do it, then you leave it. If you even torn it from the -- Could the usher assist Mr. Novakovic in handing out the notes to Mr. Weber. Mr. Weber, will I take it that you will make a photocopy and ... Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution makes a motion to compel production of the typewritten statements and any statements that have been taken by the Defence with respect to this witness. We have been prejudiced in multiple ways due to the notice with respect to this witness. The witness has now clearly testified there were notes being taken, that he did meet with the Defence on a number of occasions, that these notes were being taken contemporaneously to him making statements. So we ask for immediate production, preferably within the next hour, of any statements that were taken from this witness. Further to that, the Prosecution would also reference our urgent motion pursuant to Rule 67 of 21 June 2011 and our addendum filed on the 21st September 2011. Prosecution submits that this is it yet another example of a manner in which we are being prejudiced by the lack of disclosure of statements from the Defence. Urgent resolution of this motion would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're working hard on it at this moment, Mr. Weber. Mr. Jordash, the request is to provide within one hour the written notes written when interviewing the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We oppose for the reasons that we've outlined in the various -- in the two exchanges of pleadings, and, two, we would submit that the Prosecution have to do more than simply say, We have been prejudiced. In the same way that when we sought to complain about lack of notice, we were requested to outline the precise prejudice such as loss of investigation opportunities and so on. That is what is required at the very minimum before any cause of action arises, we would submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, throughout the testimony of this witness so far I have made a number of objections relating to the notice and the prejudice that we've suffered as a result which have included exactly what Mr. Jordash has just said, the inability to investigate. There's been discussion of a rather significant meeting that occurred in November 1994 that involved key persons which was clearly discussed beforehand. There's complete topics that this witness appears to have discussed with the Defence well before his arrival in The Hague that we knew nothing about that also involved documents that were in the possession of the Defence, translated by the Defence back in April 2011, which would correspond immediately to after when they met with this witness and have not been provided to us until immediately prior to the testimony of this witness. We're being served with a comment chart on the eve, the very eve of the testimony of the witness, and on top of it, this witness has failed to mention Operation Thompson whatsoever, and we want to know what he has to offer with regarding this. It is the -- what is prominently figures in the witness notice. And we are being prejudiced at this time by not having these statements for all the reasons outlined by Mr. Jordash and the additional reasons that I've just stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, before you respond, are those notes in your possession?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are they typewritten, handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Typewritten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us any indication about the number of pages, what are we talking about approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Approximately, I think -- from memory I think about 10 to 15 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Apart from how we further develop, you should keep them at this moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please -- you have an opportunity to further respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I would respond only briefly, which is, if the issue is that the Prosecution have been surprised by evidence, notes which deal with those issues doesn't help them. It doesn't deal with the surprise. It doesn't enable them any more so to go out into the field and investigate. It's an application which is simply a continuation of the previous applications to get the notes, but hooked onto an issue which, in reality, has got nothing to do with the notes. My learned friend's application, if he has been genuinely prejudiced, and we submit he hasn't, is to ask for time to investigate the new issues, which, as he indicates, have arisen in the courtroom not to ask for notes which corroborate or otherwise that new evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider it. Mr. Weber, you asked for within one hour. I do understand that if the Chamber would decide that you're entitled to receive those notes, it should be done on short notice. That's clear. We'll consider the matter with priority. But not within the next two minutes. The two minutes you still have available to put additional questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's understood. The Prosecution would just like to add the one point that the significance of the notes relates to much more than what Mr. Jordash said. It relates to our ability to be in a position to ascertain the truth and effectively examine this witness as to his statements and any knowledge that he might have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I thought there were two rounds of arguments and that you were invited to put additional questions to the witness and not to re-start the -- the debate. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, for clarity, can you confirm that you were assigned to the 1st Administration of the Uzice sector of the State Security Service between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in the centre in Uzice from the 1st of February, 1997 [as interpreted]. That's the administration for counter-intelligence. That was that line of work, the equivalent of it in the centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I'm looking at the clock. I know that two minutes was not much, but ... Mr. Novakovic, we'll adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back -- let me just check. We'd like to see you back tomorrow, Thursday, the 6th of the October, at 9.00 in the morning. I do instruct you hereby not to speak or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given. If at all possible we would like to see whether we could finish the testimony of this witness tomorrow. I know that you were asking for three to four hours and that not much was left today. We're not scheduled to sit on Friday. If could you try to keep it at the lower end, Mr. Weber, then we might achieve that. At the same time, if you raise your eyebrows in this respect, I can imagine, because the way in which the Stanisic Defence made its estimates and its assessment about the time needed, quite a few surprises, and the Chamber wouldn't want to make a standard that we multiply everything with three if we get estimates. We adjourn for the day. We'll resume tomorrow, 6th of October, 9.00 in the morning, in this same courtroom, II.
